title: Eikev: open the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16)
hookLine: "circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked"

cards: Chapter ten opens in the aftermath of the golden calf. Moses has just recalled the first tablets, thrown down and broken before the people's eyes.
Then God tells him: carve two new tablets like the first, and come back up. He does. And the rabbis add a detail the Torah only hints at.

In the Talmud they teach that the broken pieces weren't thrown away. They were placed in the ark, beside the whole tablets. A few verses later, Moses tells the people what has to change in them so it doesn't happen again.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked." It's a jarring image, and it's meant to be.
The Hebrew word is orlah, and readers hear in it a covering, something that closes over and blocks. The Bible uses the same root for other blocked organs.
Back in Exodus, Moses called himself a man of uncircumcised lips, his mouth closed, he felt, to speech. The prophet Jeremiah speaks of ears that are uncircumcised, that can't hear.
So an uncircumcised heart is a heart with a layer over it. It knows things, but they don't get in. Then the second half: be no more stiffnecked.

The picture, as some readers take it, comes from the farm: an ox that stiffens its neck won't turn where the driver leads. And it echoes what God called the people at the golden calf: a stiffnecked people.
So Moses is naming the old problem in two pictures. A covered heart doesn't let anything in.
A stiff neck won't turn toward anything. Notice who's asked to do the opening. Here, it's the people: you circumcise your heart.
Later in Deuteronomy, in chapter thirty, the same image comes back, and this time it's God who promises to do it for them.
Commentators hold both: the opening is your work, and it's also a gift. The broken tablets in the ark make the same point. What cracked can be carried.
A heart can be opened again.

how: Some Jewish teachers read this verse together with Deuteronomy 30:6 and the Talmud's teaching that the broken tablets were kept in the ark, as images of repentance, especially in the weeks leading up to the High Holy Days.

o: because: the opening word of the portion
a stiff neck that refuses to turn
a rope that ties the people together

games.q: inside the image — tap the pairs.
p: kept in the ark, the Talmud says

s: the word orlah in this verse is used only for the body
the Bible also speaks of uncircumcised lips and ears: blocked, closed.
stiffnecked is the word used about the golden calf
God calls the people stiffnecked there, and Moses echoes it.
in chapter thirty, God promises to do the opening
the same image returns, as a promise.

games.q: you're Moses. the first tablets lie shattered after the golden calf. what does God tell you to do?
o: carve two new tablets like the first, and come back up.
games.why: he carves new tablets. and the Talmud says the broken pieces were kept in the ark beside the whole ones.

practice: Let your shoulders drop and notice your neck, the actual muscles, and let it loosen a little. Bring to mind one person you've closed over; you don't have to forgive anything, only notice the layer.
Hold one true thing about them for a few breaths, and let your neck turn toward them, just slightly.

wordCard.voice: Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion where new tablets are carved, the broken ones kept, and a covered heart is told to open.

orig.note: Hebrew: the foreskin, the covering, of your heart. orlah is also used of lips and ears that are closed.

carryVoice: Your line: open the heart. A stiff neck can learn to turn. That's day four hundred ninety-five.

sources.q: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked.
